(a) iter948 RECONCILE HOLDS: r07 L37 now reads the CORRECTED framing verbatim — 'What to watch for: if GROUP BY has high cardinality (e.g., GROUP BY user_id across 50M users), the engine has to keep all distinct groups in memory. To actually cut that memory you must reduce the INPUT rows that reach the aggregation — add a WHERE filter on a partition/filter column so fewer rows are read, or pre-aggregate in stages (e.g. a daily rollup table). A HAVING COUNT(*) > N does not help here: HAVING runs after all groups are built, so it only trims the OUTPUT rows, not the in-memory group set the engine had to construct.' It is NO LONGER the old 'Add a HAVING COUNT(*) > N to trim' wording. Fully consistent with r23 §8 L2552 header + L2643 rationale. HAVING runs after aggregation — every row contributes to the group, then the group is discarded.' + Bad/Good examples L2645-2660 + L2662 'Use HAVING only for conditions on aggregates themselves'; clause-eval order r07 L390 WHERE->GROUP BY->HAVING->SELECT->ORDER BY. BUT the SPECIFIC perf nuance the directive asked about — an explicit card stating 'HAVING does NOT reduce aggregation/GROUP-BY working-set memory; use WHERE to cut rows pre-aggregation' — is ABSENT (no resource states the working-set-memory nuance verbatim). WORSE: r07 L37 actively teaches the OPPOSITE folklore: 'if GROUP BY has high cardinality... the engine has to keep all distinct groups in memory. Add a HAVING COUNT(*) > N to trim, or pre-aggregate.' That framing implies HAVING shrinks the grouping working-set, which it does NOT (every row still flows into every group before HAVING runs; HAVING only trims OUTPUT rows, not the build-side hash-aggregation memory). CONSEQUENCE FOR FUTURE TRIAGE: a 3rd recurrence of the 'HAVING trims memory' folklore would be a FINDABLE-GAP (nuance absent) NOT a responder-slip — and r07 L37 is a latent SOURCE of the folklore that a keyword search on 'GROUP BY high cardinality memory' / 'reduce GROUP BY memory' would surface.
